**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me he was leaving. Not in anger, not in tears—just a quiet sentence, delivered over a half-eaten plate of scrambled eggs. *"I can’t stay."* Three words, and suddenly the air in the kitchen was thicker, like the humidity before a storm. I could *feel* them pressing down on my chest, a physical force. I was eight.

Words are supposed to be light, aren’t they? Just vibrations in the air, ink on a page. But some of them linger. Some of them *stay*. They burrow into your ribs and make a home there, whispering to you in the dark.

II.

I used to collect words like other kids collected stamps or Pokémon cards. I’d write them down in a notebook—a blue one with a cracked spine—each one a tiny treasure. *"Petrichor."* The smell of rain on dry earth. *"Sonder."* The realization that every passerby has a life as vivid as your own. *"Limerence."* The intoxicating, painful crush of unrequited love.

But words can turn on you. *"Limerence"* became a knife in my side the summer I turned sixteen, when the boy I loved—who smelled like cigarette smoke and cheap cologne—told me, *"You’re like a sister to me."* The word *"sister"* tasted like ash.

III.

There’s a myth that Eskimos have fifty words for snow. (They don’t, not really—it’s a linguistic oversimplification, a white lie told to make a point.) But I like the idea. That a thing can be so vast, so present in your life, that you need a hundred different ways to describe it.

What if we had fifty words for grief?

One for the kind that sits in your throat like a stone.
One for the kind that makes your hands shake when you see their favorite color.
One for the kind that fades into background noise, like the hum of a refrigerator—always there, but easy to ignore until it stops.

IV.

I had a professor in college who said, *"Language is how we lie to ourselves."* He was a cynical man, all sharp angles and bitter coffee breath. But he wasn’t wrong. We say *"I’m fine"* when we’re breaking. We say *"It’s complicated"* when we mean *"I’m terrified."* We say *"I love you"* sometimes because we mean it, and sometimes because we’re afraid of silence.

The most dangerous words are the ones we don’t say.

V.

I once read about a study where people were asked to hold a heavy clipboard while estimating a stranger’s weight. Those holding the heavier clipboard guessed the stranger weighed more. The researchers called it *"embodied cognition"*—the idea that our bodies shape our thoughts.

What if words work the same way? What if the weight of a sentence changes how we carry it?

*"You’re not enough."* (A boulder.)
*"I believe in you."* (A feather, but one that keeps you aloft.)

VI.

My mother used to tell me, *"Words are free. It’s how you use them that costs you."* She was a poet, or at least she fancied herself one. She’d stay up late scribbling in margins, crossing out lines with enough force to tear the paper. *"This one’s no good,"* she’d mutter. *"Too heavy. Too light. Not *right*."*

I think she was afraid of getting it wrong. Of saying something that couldn’t be unsaid.

VII.

There’s a Japanese word: *"Kuchisabishii."* It means eating not because you’re hungry, but because your mouth is lonely.

I wonder if we talk for the same reason. If we fill the air with words just to keep the silence from swallowing us whole.

VIII.

I had a friend who stopped speaking for a year. Not out of trauma or protest—she just… decided. She carried a notebook instead, scribbling responses in looping cursive. At first, it was infuriating. *"Just *say* it!"* I’d snap. But after a while, I started to understand. Some things *deserve* silence. Some things are too big for sound.

When she finally spoke again, it was to say, *"I missed the taste of my own voice."*

IX.

The heaviest word I know is *"goodbye."*

Not the casual kind—the *"See ya!"* tossed over a shoulder. The real ones. The ones that mean *"I won’t see you again."* The ones that mean *"I’m letting go."*

I said it to my dog the day we put him down. His name was Orion, after the constellation. *"Good boy,"* I whispered first. Then, *"Goodbye."* The second word was a stone dropped into a well. I’m still waiting to hear it hit the bottom.

X.

They say the Inuit have no word for *"war."* (Another myth, or at least an exaggeration.) But I like the idea that some things are so foreign to a culture that they don’t even have a name for them.

What if we had no word for *"hate"*? Would it still exist?

What if we had no word for *"alone"*? Would we still feel it?

XI.

I write because words are the only way I know how to hold onto things. Memories slip like water through fingers, but if I pin them down with ink, they stay. Not perfectly. Not forever. But longer than they would otherwise.

This is why I’m telling you this. Not because I expect you to understand, but because I’m afraid of forgetting.

XII.

Here’s the truth: I don’t know what I’m doing. None of us do. We’re all just stringing words together like rafts, hoping they’ll keep us afloat.

Sometimes they do.
Sometimes they sink.

But we keep talking anyway.

Because silence is heavier.
